extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and philosophers interested in scientific method and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for judging scientific explanations, hypotheses, empirical laws, and progressive phenomena; aimed at guiding inference from observation and the limits of inductive generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are probable conjectures, not proved truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The supposition ... is at best a probable conjecture, not a proved truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses cautiously: they may supply explanations (e.g., an intervening medium for motion), but without direct proof they remain conjectural and should not be accepted as established fact. Example: supposing contiguity is required for motion-transference is only a probable conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of inferring past causes when agents and laws are known
rubrics_metrics.description: Endeavoring, in conformity with known laws, to conjecture what former collocations of known agents may have given birth to individual facts still in existence is a legitimate operation of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is exemplified by geology and judicial inquiries: when causes and laws are known and based on uniformities ascertained by perfect induction, one may infer past events (e.g., origin of strata, cause of death) without invoking hypothesis beyond known agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce unknown substances, properties, or laws without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in this theory no unknown substance introduced on supposition, nor any unknown property or law ascribed to a known substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories that rely solely on known laws and agents are preferable; introducing new entities or laws increases hypothetical character and reduces evidential strength. Laplace’s nebular example is given as a theory that avoids unknown entities but may still be weak in evidence for other reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning from present effects to past causes is legitimate when grounded in known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an example of legitimate reasoning from a present effect to a possible past cause, according to the known laws of that cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inferences (e.g., Laplace’s speculation about planets arising from the sun’s atmosphere) are acceptable provided they follow from established laws, though their evidential weight may vary depending on assumptions about the constancy of laws over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proximate and remote causes in sequences of change
rubrics_metrics.description: The original projectile force which set the body moving is the remote cause of all its motion ... but the proximate cause of no motion except that which took place at the first instant. The motion at any subsequent instant is proximately caused by the motion which took place at the instant preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causal chains, identify the immediate (proximate) cause operative at each step (often the previous state of the system), rather than attributing later effects directly to the initial remote cause. This distinction matters especially for progressive phenomena like motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued action of a permanent cause produces progressive (accumulating) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever effect has been produced up to a given time, would (unless prevented) subsist permanently, and because the cause continues to operate it goes on producing more and more of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a persistent cause as equivalent to a succession of like causes introduced successively; the total effect is the sum of successive increments (composition of causes). Examples: rusting of iron, continual gravity producing accelerated motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive change in a cause yields unequal and possibly qualitative differences in accumulated effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cause does not merely continue in action, but undergoes ... a progressive change ... the quantities added are unequal, and even the quality may now be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both accumulation and the changing character of the cause (double series). Examples: seasonal temperature changes (continuance + changing solar position), planetary motion influenced by varying central force and acquired motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes: accumulated effects are sums of successive contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause which continues in action must ... be considered as a number of causes exactly similar, successively introduced, and producing by their combination the sum of the effects which they would severally produce if they acted singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies mathematical treatment (differential calculus) for continuous accumulation problems; view ongoing causes as discrete successive contributions for analysis of progressive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deductive/mathematical treatment for infinitesimal increments and continual composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the continuance of the cause influences the effect only by adding to its quantity, and since the addition takes place according to a fixed law (equal quantities in equal times), the result is capable of being computed on mathematical principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When effects accumulate by fixed small increments, apply differential calculus or deductive methods rather than purely experimental approaches; such cases are especially suited to mathematical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform succession does not imply direct causation; identify the unconditional invariable antecedent as the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not consider spring to be the cause of summer; it is evident that both are successive effects of the heat received from the sun, and that, considered merely in itself, spring might continue forever without having the slightest tendency to produce summer. As we have so often remarked, not the conditional, but the unconditional invariable antecedent is termed the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating successive stages within a progressive phenomenon as each other's causes; seek the deeper, invariant antecedent(s) that produce the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are observed uniformities not yet resolved into underlying laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific inquirers give the name of Empirical Laws to those uniformities which observation or experiment has shown to exist, but on which they hesitate to rely in cases varying much from those which have been actually observed, for want of seeing any reason why such a law should exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize empirical laws as derivative and provisional until explained deductively by more fundamental laws; they require caution when extrapolating beyond observed circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical (derivative) laws may depend on laws and on collocations of causes, limiting generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws ... mostly depend on those ultimate laws, and an ultimate fact; namely, the mode of co-existence of some of the component elements of the universe. The derivative law in this case depends not solely on laws, but on a collocation; and collocations can not be reduced to any law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws may rely on particular arrangements (collocations) of causes, they can only be safely received within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which they have been observed. Example: geological strata order on Earth need not hold on other planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone establishes only empirical law, not cause
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization amounts to more than an empirical law when the only proof on which it rests is that of the Method of Agreement. ... The method affords no means of determining which of these uniformities are laws of causation, and which are merely derivative laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer causal laws from agreement alone; use Method of Difference or deductive explanation to identify true causes. Results from mere observation without experiment remain empirical until further tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authority of empirical laws by plausibility they derive solely from laws versus collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: These empirical laws may be of greater or less authority, according as there is reason to presume that they are resolvable into laws only, or into laws and collocations together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate empirical regularities differently depending on whether they plausibly stem from a single enduring cause (higher authority, e.g., developmental stages of organisms) or from contingent collocations (lower authority, e.g., order of strata). Use this in judging how strongly to generalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious assuming constancy of natural laws over vast timescales when inferring ancient states
rubrics_metrics.description: There would still be a much greater chance of error in assuming that the existing laws of nature are the same which existed at the origin of the solar system, than in merely presuming (with geologists) that those laws have lasted through a few revolutions and transformations of a single one among the bodies of which that system is composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring events far in the past (e.g., solar system origin), explicitly acknowledge and critically assess the assumption that laws and conditions remained constant; uncertainty about such constancy weakens the evidential support of the inference.
